title: When is a coin allowed to move?
dek: nLockTime delays a transaction until a specified block height or time. Each input’s nSequence can require a minimum age for the spent output. Script opcodes can enforce these requirements.

blocks.text: A payment channel, an escrow with a deadline, a refund that must wait: each needs a coin that cannot move yet. Bitcoin gets there with four specifications from 2014 and 2015, all consensus soft forks recorded as deployed. BIP 65 lets an output demand a date or a block height. BIP 68 repurposes each input’s sequence number as a relative lock, BIP 112 lets an output demand it, and BIP 113 decides which clock time locks read.

The transaction fields and script opcodes have different jobs. A field can delay one transaction. A script condition can require the transaction to use that field. The examples below check both against Bitcoin Core’s test transactions.

figure.title: One field, two scales
figure.caption: nLockTime splits its 32 bits at 500,000,000: heights below, Unix times above. A relative lock reads the same 16 bits as blocks or as 512-second units, depending on one flag.

sections.heading: A field that does not lock a coin

blocks.text: Every transaction ends with a four-byte number, nLockTime. When enforced, it prevents inclusion until the block height or applicable block time is greater than that value. The field constrains this spending transaction. It does not prevent a different transaction from spending the same coins.

Setting nLockTime does not by itself make the coins unspendable before that time. As BIP 65 explains, another signed transaction may already spend them without a lock. A condition in the output’s script is needed to enforce the delay on the spend.

blocks.title: A field that does not lock a coin
blocks.caption: Schematic. A future nLockTime proves a spend is possible later, but another spend of the same coin may already exist; a condition in the coin’s own script closes that gap.

blocks.text: The same field carries two kinds of value. Below a threshold it is a block height; at or above it, a time. BIP 65’s code names the threshold LOCKTIME_THRESHOLD, and Bitcoin Core defines it as 500,000,000, which as a Unix time falls on 5 November 1985. Any height Bitcoin will reach for a very long time sits below that line, and any date worth locking to sits above it.

If every input has the maximum sequence number, 0xffffffff, the transaction’s nLockTime is not enforced. BIP 143’s native P2WPKH example sets nLockTime to 17 and leaves one input non-final, so no block below height 18 could include it. BIP 174’s final transaction has nLockTime 0 and only final inputs.

blocks.title: Reading published transactions
blocks.caption: Version, nLockTime and nSequence of four transactions published in BIPs 143 and 174, as consensus reads them.

sections.heading: Putting the lock in the output

blocks.text: BIP 65 closes the gap with a new opcode, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, which redefines the unused NOP2. It sits in the output’s script, so the condition travels with the coin, and it makes the output unspendable until some point in the future.

The opcode compares its argument with the spending transaction’s nLockTime. It does not read the current chain height or time. The transaction’s nLockTime must also permit inclusion in the block. Together, these checks enforce the script’s requirement. The BIP credits Gregory Maxwell with suggesting this indirect comparison.
OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY rejects the script if any of these conditions applies:

items: The argument and nLockTime use different units: block height versus time.
The argument is greater than nLockTime.

blocks.text: The last check prevents this input from disabling nLockTime. If all checks pass, execution continues as for a NOP: no further operation occurs at this opcode.

blocks.title: The lock fields, checked
blocks.caption: Twelve one-input transactions from Bitcoin Core’s test suite check script conditions against transaction fields. Passing does not establish block eligibility. The timeline shows the separate chain rule schematically; it does not use live chain data. Field changes are computed examples, not Core test cases.

blocks.text: Try the absolute cases above. An argument of 499,999,999 against nLockTime 499,999,998 fails by one block. Add one to nLockTime and it passes; add one more and nLockTime becomes a time, and the same argument now fails because the kinds no longer match.

The argument is read as a number of up to five bytes, not the usual four. BIP 65’s code explains why: four bytes would give a year 2038 problem, while nLockTime itself, an unsigned 32-bit field, only becomes meaningless after the year 2106.

The BIP’s simplest example prevents spending before an expiry time. Its script contains the expiry, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, a DROP, and an ordinary pay-to-public-key-hash check. The signature check cannot authorize a spend before the expiry requirement is met.

An absolute lock names a moment. Many protocols need something else: a delay that starts only when a coin is created. BIP 68 builds that out of each input’s nSequence field, and it does so only for transactions with version 2 or higher.

If bit 31 is set, BIP 68 does not enforce a relative lock. The value 0xffffffff still marks the input final for nLockTime. When bit 31 is clear, bit 22 selects the relative-lock unit: blocks if clear, or 512-second units if set. The low 16 bits hold the value. The mask 0x0000ffff MUST be applied to extract it. The intervening bits are reserved for future use.

blocks.title: Thirty-two bits, three jobs
blocks.caption: BIP 68’s two largest relative locks as bits: the disable flag, the type flag and the 16 value bits; the rest carry no meaning.

blocks.text: Why 512 seconds? The authors chose it because blocks arrive every 600 seconds on average, so either unit covers about the same span with the same bits. BIP 68’s own examples give the limits: up to 65,535 blocks, about 1.25 years, or a time below 33,554,431 seconds, about 1.06 years.

A block-based relative lock of n permits inclusion at the coin’s confirmation height plus n, or later. A time-based lock uses median time past (MTP), not elapsed wall-clock time. Its starting value is the MTP of the block immediately before the coin’s confirmation block. Add 512 × n seconds to get the required time. The MTP of the candidate spending block’s parent must reach or exceed that time. The coinbase input is exempt.

BIP 112 replaces NOP3 with OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY. It lets a script branch require a minimum age for the spent coin. The opcode fails if the stack is empty or the argument is negative. If the argument has bit 31 set, the opcode acts as a NOP, reserved for future soft forks.
Otherwise, the opcode compares the argument with the input’s nSequence after masking both values. It rejects the script if any of these conditions applies:

items: Bit 31 of the input’s nSequence is set.
The argument and nSequence use different units.
The masked argument is greater than the masked nSequence.

blocks.title: CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, check by check
blocks.caption: One of Bitcoin Core’s cases, a time-based relative lock, run check by check by the tested model.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: A relative lock needs both halves: a transaction version of 2 or more, and bit 31 of nSequence clear. With either missing, nSequence carries no relative lock under BIP 68, and a CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY whose argument has bit 31 clear fails rather than passing.

BIP 112 gives escrow and payment-channel examples. One escrow permits spending with two of three signatures at any time, or to Alice alone after 30 days. The delay starts when the payment into the escrow confirms. For channels, the authors argue that a relative lock gives a predictable response period for a revoked transaction. An absolute deadline would instead require closing the channel before that deadline.

Before BIP 113, time-based nLockTime used the including block’s own timestamp. Block timestamps need not increase in order. The authors identified an incentive for a miner to claim a later time and collect fees from transactions that had not matured by wall-clock time.

BIP 113 replaces that timestamp with the median of the past 11 blocks’ timestamps, the median time past, which only moves forward. The rule covers every transaction, coinbase included, and the authors expected time-locked transactions to confirm about an hour later than before. BIP 68’s time-based locks are measured in the same median time past.

blocks.title: Which clock
blocks.caption: Schematic, not chain data: block timestamps need not increase, so locks read the median of the last eleven instead.

blocks.text: The rollout is recorded in the BIPs. BIP 65 used the older switchover for version-4 blocks: enforced once 750 of the previous 1,000 blocks signalled, with older versions rejected at 950. BIPs 68, 112 and 113 were to deploy together through BIP 9 on bit 0, with a mainnet start of 1 May 2016.

blocks.label: Note
blocks.text: The figures here check fields against fields, as the opcodes do. Whether a block may include a transaction also depends on the chain’s height and median time past, which this site never sees.
